claim: The circadian clock relies on regulated degradation of clock proteins to maintain rhythmicity.
source: The circadian clock relies on regulated degradation of clock proteins to maintain rhythmicity.
evidence: This is a general statement about circadian clock function presented in the abstract.

claim: Few components that mediate protein degradation in the circadian clock are known.
source: Despite this, we know few components that mediate protein degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study in the abstract.

claim: High levels of functional redundancy exist within plant E3 ubiquitin ligase families.
source: This is due to high levels of functional redundancy within plant E3 ubiquitin ligase families.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the abstract.

claim: A library of transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing dominant-negative 'decoy' E3 ubiquitin ligases was generated.
source: In order to overcome this issue and discover E3 ubiquitin ligases that control circadian function, we generated a library of transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing dominant-negative 'decoy' E3 ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Dozens of new potential regulators of circadian function were identified through the decoy screen.
source: We determined their effects on the circadian clock and identified dozens of new potential regulators of circadian function.
evidence: This is a summary of the screening results in the abstract.

claim: MAC3A (PUB59) and MAC3B (PUB60) redundantly control circadian period by regulating splicing.
source: We show that they redundantly control circadian period by regulating splicing.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The circadian clock controls hypocotyl elongation in plants.
source: In plants, the circadian clock controls diverse aspects of plant development, including hypocotyl elongation, leaf movement, seasonal flowering time, and stress responses, both biotic and abiotic (Dowson-Day and Millar, 1999; Fowler et al., 1999; Hoshizaki and Hamner, 1964; Ingle and Roden, 2014; Liu et al., 2013; Nakamichi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The circadian clock controls leaf movement in plants.
source: In plants, the circadian clock controls diverse aspects of plant development, including hypocotyl elongation, leaf movement, seasonal flowering time, and stress responses, both biotic and abiotic (Dowson-Day and Millar, 1999; Fowler et al., 1999; Hoshizaki and Hamner, 1964; Ingle and Roden, 2014; Liu et al., 2013; Nakamichi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The circadian clock controls seasonal flowering time in plants.
source: In plants, the circadian clock controls diverse aspects of plant development, including hypocotyl elongation, leaf movement, seasonal flowering time, and stress responses, both biotic and abiotic (Dowson-Day and Millar, 1999; Fowler et al., 1999; Hoshizaki and Hamner, 1964; Ingle and Roden, 2014; Liu et al., 2013; Nakamichi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The circadian clock controls stress responses in plants.
source: In plants, the circadian clock controls diverse aspects of plant development, including hypocotyl elongation, leaf movement, seasonal flowering time, and stress responses, both biotic and abiotic (Dowson-Day and Millar, 1999; Fowler et al., 1999; Hoshizaki and Hamner, 1964; Ingle and Roden, 2014; Liu et al., 2013; Nakamichi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The circadian clock is capable of maintaining roughly 24 hr rhythms in the absence of environmental signals.
source: The timing of the clock is set by environmental inputs, such as daily changes in light and temperature, but it is also self-sustaining and capable of maintaining roughly 24 hr rhythms in the absence of changes in the environmental signals.
evidence: This is a fundamental property of circadian clocks.

claim: Self-sustaining oscillations of the circadian clock are driven by interlocking transcriptional feedback loops.
source: These self-sustaining oscillations are driven by interlocking transcriptional feedback loops that result in successive expression of a series of transcriptional repressors and activators throughout the day (McClung, 2014; Ronald and Davis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: CCA1 and LHY are morning expressed transcriptional repressors in the plant circadian clock.
source: These are the morning expressed CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1 (CCA1) and LATE ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL (LHY), the morning and afternoon expressed PSEUDO-RESPONSE REGULATOR (PRR) family, and the evening expressed evening complex (including EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3), EARLY FLOWERING 4 (ELF4) and LUX ARRYTHMO (LUX)) (Alabadí et al., 2001; Alabadí et al., 2002; Carré and Kim, 2002; Doyle et al., 2002; Farré et al., 2005; Fujimori et al., 2005; Gendron et al., 2012; Hazen et al., 2005; Helfer et al., 2011; Hicks et al., 1996; Hicks et al., 2001; Kikis et al., 2005; Mizoguchi et al., 2002; Nakamichi et al., 2005b; Nakamichi et al., 2005a; Onai and Ishiura, 2005; Schaffer et al., 1998; Wang and Tobin, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The PRR family are morning and afternoon expressed transcriptional repressors in the plant circadian clock.
source: These are the morning expressed CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1 (CCA1) and LATE ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL (LHY), the morning and afternoon expressed PSEUDO-RESPONSE REGULATOR (PRR) family, and the evening expressed evening complex (including EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3), EARLY FLOWERING 4 (ELF4) and LUX ARRYTHMO (LUX)) (Alabadí et al., 2001; Alabadí et al., 2002; Carré and Kim, 2002; Doyle et al., 2002; Farré et al., 2005; Fujimori et al., 2005; Gendron et al., 2012; Hazen et al., 2005; Helfer et al., 2011; Hicks et al., 1996; Hicks et al., 2001; Kikis et al., 2005; Mizoguchi et al., 2002; Nakamichi et al., 2005b; Nakamichi et al., 2005a; Onai and Ishiura, 2005; Schaffer et al., 1998; Wang and Tobin, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The evening complex (ELF3, ELF4, and LUX) are evening expressed transcriptional repressors in the plant circadian clock.
source: These are the morning expressed CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1 (CCA1) and LATE ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL (LHY), the morning and afternoon expressed PSEUDO-RESPONSE REGULATOR (PRR) family, and the evening expressed evening complex (including EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3), EARLY FLOWERING 4 (ELF4) and LUX ARRYTHMO (LUX)) (Alabadí et al., 2001; Alabadí et al., 2002; Carré and Kim, 2002; Doyle et al., 2002; Farré et al., 2005; Fujimori et al., 2005; Gendron et al., 2012; Hazen et al., 2005; Helfer et al., 2011; Hicks et al., 1996; Hicks et al., 2001; Kikis et al., 2005; Mizoguchi et al., 2002; Nakamichi et al., 2005b; Nakamichi et al., 2005a; Onai and Ishiura, 2005; Schaffer et al., 1998; Wang and Tobin, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: LWD, RVE, and LNK genes are critical transcriptional activators in the plant clock.
source: More recently, the LIGHT-REGULATED WD (LWD), REVEILLE (RVE), and NIGHT LIGHT–INDUCIBLE AND CLOCK-REGULATED1 (LNK) genes, were identified as critical transcriptional activators in the plant clock and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the transcriptional feedback loops that drive oscillations (Farinas and Mas, 2011; Hsu et al., 2013; Rawat et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Eukaryotic circadian clocks employ the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) to degrade clock transcription factors at the appropriate time of day.
source: Eukaryotic circadian clocks employ the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) to degrade clock transcription factors at the appropriate time of day (Grima et al., 2002; He et al., 2003; Ito et al., 2012; Ko et al., 2002; Shirogane et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The UPS can mediate protein degradation quickly and specifically.
source: The UPS is ideally suited for regulation of the circadian clock because it can mediate protein degradation quickly and specifically.
evidence: This is a general property of the UPS.

claim: E3 ubiquitin ligases act as substrate adaptor proteins by bringing the substrate into proximity of an E2 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme to promote substrate ubiquitylation.
source: E3 ubiquitin ligases act as substrate adaptor proteins by bringing the substrate into proximity of an E2 ubiquitin conjugating enzyme to promote substrate ubiquitylation.
evidence: This describes the general mechanism of E3 ligases.

claim: Once a lysine-48-linked poly-ubiquitin chain is added to the substrate, it is sent to the proteasome where it is degraded.
source: Once a lysine-48-linked poly-ubiquitin chain is added to the substrate, it is sent to the proteasome where it is degraded (Vierstra, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: E3 ubiquitin ligases coordinate ubiquitylation that regulates processes such as endocytosis or the formation of protein complexes.
source: In addition to their role in the ubiquitin proteasome system, E3 ubiquitin ligases also coordinate ubiquitylation that regulates other processes, such as endocytosis or the formation of protein complexes (Komander and Rape, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: F-box proteins are utilized by all eukaryotic circadian clocks.
source: F-box proteins are the substrate adaptor component of a larger E3 ubiquitin ligase complex and are utilized by all eukaryotic circadian clocks (Grima et al., 2002; He et al., 2003; Ito et al., 2012; Ko et al., 2002; Shirogane et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The SCF complex consists of SKP1, CULLIN, RBX1, and the F-box protein.
source: The complex, abbreviated SCF, consists of S PHASE KINASE-ASSOCIATED PROTEIN 1 (SKP1), CULLIN, RING-BOX1 (RBX1), and the F-box protein (Bai et al., 1996; Deshaies, 1999; Deshaies and Joazeiro, 2009; Hua and Vierstra, 2011; Lechner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ZTL, LKP2, and FKF1 are a family of three partially redundant F-box proteins that regulate the circadian clock and flowering time in plants.
source: A family of three partially redundant F-box proteins, ZEITLUPE (ZTL), LOV KELCH PROTEIN 2 (LKP2), and FLAVIN-BINDING KELCH REPEAT 1 (FKF1), regulate the circadian clock and flowering time in plants (Imaizumi et al., 2005; Imaizumi et al., 2003; Nelson et al., 2000; Schultz et al., 2001; Somers et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ZTL regulates stability of TOC1, PRR5, and CHE.
source: ZTL, which has the largest impact on clock function, regulates stability of TOC1, PRR5, and CHE (Fujiwara et al., 2008; Kiba et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2018; Más et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: LHY stability is regulated by the non-F-box RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase SINAT5.
source: Outside of the ZTL family, some evidence suggests that LHY stability is regulated by the non-F-box RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase SINAT5 (Park et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Little progress has been made in identifying additional E3 ubiquitin ligases that participate in clock function since the discovery of ZTL family and SINAT5.
source: Since the discovery of these E3 ubiquitin ligases, little progress has been made in identifying additional E3 ubiquitin ligases that participate in clock function.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study.

claim: The inability to identify plant E3 ubiquitin ligases that regulate the circadian clock is likely due to genetic challenges that hamper traditional forward genetic approaches.
source: The inability to identify plant E3 ubiquitin ligases that regulate the circadian clock is likely due to genetic challenges that hamper traditional forward genetic approaches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the challenges described.

claim: Gene duplication has led to expansion of the genes involved in UPS function in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis, gene duplication has led to expansion of the genes involved in UPS function (Navarro-Quezada et al., 2013; Risseeuw et al., 2003; Yee and Goring, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There are approximately 700 Arabidopsis F-box genes.
source: For instance, there are approximately 700 Arabidopsis F-box genes, while in humans there are 69 (Finn et al., 2016; Grima et al., 2002; Kuroda et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There are 69 F-box genes in humans.
source: For instance, there are approximately 700 Arabidopsis F-box genes, while in humans there are 69 (Finn et al., 2016; Grima et al., 2002; Kuroda et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Gene expansion has likely led to increased functional redundancy rendering gene knockouts an inefficient method to identify function.
source: This has likely led to increased functional redundancy rendering gene knockouts an inefficient method to identify function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expansion.

claim: The majority of ztl mutant alleles are semi-dominant.
source: To support this, the majority of ztl mutant alleles are semi-dominant (Kevei et al., 2006; Martin-Tryon et al., 2007; Somers et al., 2004; Somers et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Reverse genetic strategies may be a more potent approach to identify E3 ubiquitin ligases that regulate clock function.
source: This suggests that reverse genetic strategies may be a more potent approach to identify E3 ubiquitin ligases that regulate clock function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the semi-dominant nature of ztl mutants.

claim: The decoy approach involves expressing an E3 ubiquitin ligase that lacks the ability to recruit the E2 conjugating enzyme but retains the ability to bind to the substrate.
source: The decoy approach involves expressing an E3 ubiquitin ligase that lacks the ability to recruit the E2 conjugating enzyme but retains the ability to bind to the substrate (Han et al., 2004; Kishi and Yamao, 1998; Latres et al., 1999; Li et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The decoy inactivates the full-length E3 ubiquitin ligase and acts to stabilize the substrate protein.
source: We have shown that this inactivates the full-length E3 ubiquitin ligase and acts to stabilize the substrate protein (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The decoy acts as a dominant-negative.
source: The decoy acts as a dominant-negative, making it an effective genetic tool to identify the function of redundant E3 ubiquitin ligases.
evidence: This is a characterization of the decoy approach.

claim: The decoy stabilizes interaction with substrate proteins.
source: Additionally, the decoy stabilizes interaction with substrate proteins.
evidence: This is a property of the decoy approach.

claim: The completed library contains nearly ¼ of the Arabidopsis E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: Our completed library contains nearly ¼ of the Arabidopsis E3 ubiquitin ligases (Vierstra, 2009), spanning sixteen different protein-protein interaction domain classes, and including many genes with known functions as well as many that have not been studied in detail previously.
evidence: This describes the scope of the library created.

claim: The decoy library spans sixteen different protein-protein interaction domain classes.
source: Our completed library contains nearly ¼ of the Arabidopsis E3 ubiquitin ligases (Vierstra, 2009), spanning sixteen different protein-protein interaction domain classes, and including many genes with known functions as well as many that have not been studied in detail previously.
evidence: This describes the diversity of the library.

claim: A surprisingly large number of genes regulate clock function with minor effects.
source: We uncovered a surprisingly large number of genes that regulate clock function with minor effects and a smaller number with more dramatic effects on clock period or phase.
evidence: This is a summary of the screening results.

claim: A smaller number of genes have more dramatic effects on clock period or phase.
source: We uncovered a surprisingly large number of genes that regulate clock function with minor effects and a smaller number with more dramatic effects on clock period or phase.
evidence: This is a summary of the screening results.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B have been previously implicated in splicing.
source: We then perform focused genetic studies on PLANT U-BOX 59 and PLANT U-BOX 60 (MAC3A and MAC3B), two homologous U-box genes which have been previously implicated in splicing.
evidence: This is stated as background for the follow-up studies.

claim: PRR9 is mis-spliced in the mac3a/mac3b double mutant.
source: We go on to determine their molecular function in the clock by showing that the core clock gene, PRR9, is mis-spliced in the mac3a/mac3b double mutant.
evidence: This is a key finding from the follow-up studies.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B are the first U-box-type E3 ligases involved in clock function in any system.
source: This work demonstrates the effectiveness of the decoy technique as a screening platform and identifies the first U-box-type E3 ligases that are involved in clock function in any system.
evidence: This is stated as a key contribution of the work.

claim: 82% of the attempted F-box genes were successfully cloned.
source: In fact, we were able to clone 82% of the attempted F-box genes, and ultimately succeeded in isolating transgenic plants for 65% of cloned decoy F-boxes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cloning process.

claim: Transgenic plants were isolated for 65% of cloned decoy F-boxes.
source: In fact, we were able to clone 82% of the attempted F-box genes, and ultimately succeeded in isolating transgenic plants for 65% of cloned decoy F-boxes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the transformation process.

claim: Transgenic plants were generated expressing 65% of the U-box family.
source: We also generated transgenic plants expressing 65% of the U-box family (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the transformation process.

claim: 30% of successfully generated F-box transgenics contained an LRR domain.
source: Of those successfully generated transgenics, the majority contained either an LRR, Kelch, or F-box Associated (FBA1, FBA3, or FBD) protein recognition domain (at 30%, 24%, or 30%, respectively), with some F-box proteins containing both LRR and FBD domains together (14%) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 24% of successfully generated F-box transgenics contained a Kelch domain.
source: Of those successfully generated transgenics, the majority contained either an LRR, Kelch, or F-box Associated (FBA1, FBA3, or FBD) protein recognition domain (at 30%, 24%, or 30%, respectively), with some F-box proteins containing both LRR and FBD domains together (14%) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 30% of successfully generated F-box transgenics contained an F-box Associated domain.
source: Of those successfully generated transgenics, the majority contained either an LRR, Kelch, or F-box Associated (FBA1, FBA3, or FBD) protein recognition domain (at 30%, 24%, or 30%, respectively), with some F-box proteins containing both LRR and FBD domains together (14%) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 14% of successfully generated F-box transgenics contained both LRR and FBD domains together.
source: Of those successfully generated transgenics, the majority contained either an LRR, Kelch, or F-box Associated (FBA1, FBA3, or FBD) protein recognition domain (at 30%, 24%, or 30%, respectively), with some F-box proteins containing both LRR and FBD domains together (14%) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 25% of successfully generated F-box transgenics contained no known protein recognition domain.
source: The remaining F-boxes contained a small number of other domains (6%), including TUBBY-like or WD40 domains, or no known protein recognition domain (25%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the library characterization.

claim: 55% of cloned U-box genes contained ARM repeats.
source: Of those cloned, 55% contained ARM repeats, 10% contained a Protein Kinase domain, 7.5% contained only a coiled coil region, 5% contained a WD repeat, 5% contained other annotated domains, and 17.5% contained no annotated domains (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 10% of cloned U-box genes contained a Protein Kinase domain.
source: Of those cloned, 55% contained ARM repeats, 10% contained a Protein Kinase domain, 7.5% contained only a coiled coil region, 5% contained a WD repeat, 5% contained other annotated domains, and 17.5% contained no annotated domains (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 7.5% of cloned U-box genes contained only a coiled coil region.
source: Of those cloned, 55% contained ARM repeats, 10% contained a Protein Kinase domain, 7.5% contained only a coiled coil region, 5% contained a WD repeat, 5% contained other annotated domains, and 17.5% contained no annotated domains (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 5% of cloned U-box genes contained a WD repeat.
source: Of those cloned, 55% contained ARM repeats, 10% contained a Protein Kinase domain, 7.5% contained only a coiled coil region, 5% contained a WD repeat, 5% contained other annotated domains, and 17.5% contained no annotated domains (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 17.5% of cloned U-box genes contained no annotated domains.
source: Of those cloned, 55% contained ARM repeats, 10% contained a Protein Kinase domain, 7.5% contained only a coiled coil region, 5% contained a WD repeat, 5% contained other annotated domains, and 17.5% contained no annotated domains (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Five individual plants had an RAE greater than 0.6 which signifies lack of rhythmicity.
source: Five individual plants had an RAE greater than 0.6 which signifies lack of rhythmicity (Figures 2–3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the rhythmicity analysis shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: No control plants had an RAE greater than 0.6.
source: In comparison, no control plants (n = 1783) had an RAE greater than 0.6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the control analysis shown in figure supplements.

claim: No decoy populations had more than one arrhythmic plant.
source: No decoy populations had more than one arrhythmic plant, making it unlikely that any decoy ablates clock function.
evidence: This is an observation from the rhythmicity analysis.

claim: Most decoy expressing populations showed a significant phase advance when compared to the wild type.
source: Interestingly, we observed a phase shift in most of our decoy expressing populations when compared to the wild type, with the large majority showing a significant phase advance (Figures 4–5).
evidence: This is an observation from the phase analysis shown in Figures 4-5.

claim: The approximately 1 hr advance in phase appeared to be a general effect of transgene expression.
source: This approximately 1 hr advance in phase (compare to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) appeared to be a general effect of transgene expression in our experiments, suggesting the phase of the CCA1p::Luciferase is particularly sensitive to transgene overexpression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the phase data comparing to figure supplements.

claim: 40 F-box decoy populations cause a statistically significant change in phase.
source: Using this method, we found that 40 F-box decoy populations cause a statistically significant change in phase (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 1.94 × 10−4), equating to approximately 22% of tested populations (Figure 4, marked with stars and blue gene names).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 22% of tested F-box populations had statistically significant phase changes.
source: Using this method, we found that 40 F-box decoy populations cause a statistically significant change in phase (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 1.94 × 10−4), equating to approximately 22% of tested populations (Figure 4, marked with stars and blue gene names).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis.

claim: 37 out of 40 F-box decoy populations with phase differences had minor phase differences (<2 hr).
source: Based on this definition, many of the F-box decoy populations had minor phase differences (37/40 populations) while only three (AT5G48980 – 2.36 hr delayed, AT5G44980 – 2.16 hr delayed, and AT5G42350 – 2.16 hr advanced) had major phase differences.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase analysis.

claim: Three F-box decoy populations had major phase differences (>2 hr).
source: Based on this definition, many of the F-box decoy populations had minor phase differences (37/40 populations) while only three (AT5G48980 – 2.36 hr delayed, AT5G44980 – 2.16 hr delayed, and AT5G42350 – 2.16 hr advanced) had major phase differences.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase analysis.

claim: AT5G48980 decoy population had a 2.36 hr delayed phase.
source: Based on this definition, many of the F-box decoy populations had minor phase differences (37/40 populations) while only three (AT5G48980 – 2.36 hr delayed, AT5G44980 – 2.16 hr delayed, and AT5G42350 – 2.16 hr advanced) had major phase differences.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase analysis.

claim: AT5G44980 decoy population had a 2.16 hr delayed phase.
source: Based on this definition, many of the F-box decoy populations had minor phase differences (37/40 populations) while only three (AT5G48980 – 2.36 hr delayed, AT5G44980 – 2.16 hr delayed, and AT5G42350 – 2.16 hr advanced) had major phase differences.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase analysis.

claim: AT5G42350 decoy population had a 2.16 hr advanced phase.
source: Based on this definition, many of the F-box decoy populations had minor phase differences (37/40 populations) while only three (AT5G48980 – 2.36 hr delayed, AT5G44980 – 2.16 hr delayed, and AT5G42350 – 2.16 hr advanced) had major phase differences.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase analysis.

claim: Three U-box decoy populations have phase differences.
source: In addition to the F-box decoys, three of the U-box decoy populations have phase differences (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 1.00 × 10−3), none of which had major phase differences (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: None of the U-box decoy populations with phase differences had major phase differences.
source: In addition to the F-box decoys, three of the U-box decoy populations have phase differences (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 1.00 × 10−3), none of which had major phase differences (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phase analysis.

claim: ACF1 contains both an F-box associated domain (FBD) and Leucine rich repeats (LRR).
source: ACF1, which contains both an F-box associated domain (FBD) and Leucine rich repeats (LRR), has no publications detailing its function.
evidence: This is a description of the protein domains in ACF1.

claim: ACF1 has no publications detailing its function.
source: ACF1, which contains both an F-box associated domain (FBD) and Leucine rich repeats (LRR), has no publications detailing its function.
evidence: This is stated as background information.

claim: ACF1 has a close homolog AT5G44960 with an E-value of 1.60 × 10−146.
source: The absence of an identified phenotype may be due to the existence of a close homolog (AT5G44960 – E-value of 1.60 × 10−146, Table 1), as higher order mutants or dominant negative technology, such as the decoy technique, may be required to uncover its function.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: ACF1 is not regulated by either light cycles or the circadian clock.
source: ACF1 is not regulated by either light cycles or the circadian clock, as the correlation value, a measure of the similarity between the expression data and the hypothesized cycling pattern, is less than the standard correlation cutoff of 0.8 (Mockler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression data analysis with a citation.

claim: ACF1 is expressed globally, although there may be some enrichment in senescent leaves or anthers.
source: Tissue expression maps suggest that ACF1 is expressed globally, although there may be some enrichment in senescent leaves or anthers (Klepikova et al., 2016; Winter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression atlas data with citations.

claim: ACF2 contains a Kelch repeat.
source: We performed the same analysis on ACF2, which contains a Kelch repeat.
evidence: This is a description of the protein domain in ACF2.

claim: ACF2 has a close homolog AT5G48990 with an E-value of 1.10 × 10−124.
source: No publications are available, possibly due to the existence of a close homolog (AT5G48990 – E-value of 1.10 × 10−124, Table 1), although ACF2 was described in a manuscript discussing the prevalence of the Kelch-repeat containing F-box proteins in Arabidopsis (Andrade et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: ACF2 was described in a manuscript discussing the prevalence of the Kelch-repeat containing F-box proteins in Arabidopsis.
source: No publications are available, possibly due to the existence of a close homolog (AT5G48990 – E-value of 1.10 × 10−124, Table 1), although ACF2 was described in a manuscript discussing the prevalence of the Kelch-repeat containing F-box proteins in Arabidopsis (Andrade et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Diurnal and circadian expression data was not available for ACF2.
source: Diurnal and circadian expression data was not available for this gene (Mockler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on database searches with a citation.

claim: ACF2 shows predominant expression in seed.
source: While data on ACF2 expression is unavailable in one expression map, the second shows predominant expression in seed (Klepikova et al., 2016; Winter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression atlas data with citations.

claim: CFK1 is expressed globally.
source: While temporal expression data is unavailable, expression maps demonstrate that CFK1 is expressed globally (Table 1) (Klepikova et al., 2016; Mockler et al., 2007; Winter et al., 2007), suggesting it is not tissue specific.
evidence: This is based on expression atlas data with citations.

claim: cfk1 knockout mutants cause decreased hypocotyl length.
source: cfk1 knockout mutants cause decreased hypocotyl length, and interact with the CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 9 (COP9) Signalosome (Franciosini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: CFK1 interacts with the COP9 Signalosome.
source: cfk1 knockout mutants cause decreased hypocotyl length, and interact with the CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 9 (COP9) Signalosome (Franciosini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: CFK1 has a very close homolog AT5G42360 (CFK2) with an E-value of 3.6 × 10−298.
source: CFK1 has a very close homolog (AT5G42360, also known as CFK2 – E-value of 3.6 × 10−298), but while it cannot be completely redundant with CFK1 because of the knockout phenotype, reduction in the levels of both genes increases the phenotypic severity (Franciosini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis with a citation.

claim: Reduction in the levels of both CFK1 and CFK2 increases the phenotypic severity.
source: CFK1 has a very close homolog (AT5G42360, also known as CFK2 – E-value of 3.6 × 10−298), but while it cannot be completely redundant with CFK1 because of the knockout phenotype, reduction in the levels of both genes increases the phenotypic severity (Franciosini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: CFK1 expression is induced by light.
source: CFK1 is expression induced by light (Franciosini et al., 2013), providing strength to the argument that it could be involved in clock function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: 36 F-box decoy populations have significantly different periods than the control.
source: From this analysis we found that 36 F-box decoy populations have significantly different periods than the control (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 2.55 × 10−4) (Figure 6, marked with stars and green gene names).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: 19% of tested F-box populations had significantly different periods.
source: These correspond to approximately 19% of tested populations (Figure 6, marked with stars and green gene names).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis.

claim: Only one F-box decoy population has a major period difference (>1 hr).
source: Interestingly, only one F-box decoy population has a major period difference (AT1G20800 – 1.02 hr longer than the wild type).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the period analysis.

claim: AT1G20800 decoy population has a period 1.02 hr longer than the wild type.
source: Interestingly, only one F-box decoy population has a major period difference (AT1G20800 – 1.02 hr longer than the wild type).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the period analysis.

claim: Two F-box decoy populations are not different than the control as a whole population, but have distinct subpopulations that are different than the control.
source: There are two F-box decoy populations that are not different than the control as a whole population, but have distinct subpopulations that are different than the control (Figure 6, marked with daggers and blue gene names).
evidence: This is a result from subpopulation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: AT2G44030 has a subpopulation with an average period 4.1 hr longer than the control.
source: One, AT2G44030, has a subpopulation that has a major effect on period, containing four plants with an average period 4.1 hr longer than the control.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from subpopulation analysis.

claim: AT1G50870 has a minor effect on the period overall (0.57 hr longer).
source: A second decoy population, AT1G50870, which has a minor effect on the period overall (0.57 hr longer) also contains two separable subpopulations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from period analysis.

claim: AT1G50870 has a subpopulation with a major effect on the period (2.8 hr longer).
source: One subpopulation has a major effect on the period (2.8 hr longer, n = 5), while the second has a minor effect (0.36 hr longer, n = 55).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from subpopulation analysis.

claim: Only three of the 41 identified F-box populations or subpopulations had shorter periods than the wildtype.
source: Only three of the 41 identified populations or subpopulations had shorter periods than the wildtype.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from period analysis.

claim: AT1G76920 has a period 0.76 hr shorter than wildtype.
source: AT1G76920 and AT1G51320 both have shorter periods overall (0.76 and 0.29 hr shorter, respectively), while AT1G09650 has a subpopulation that is 0.61 hr shorter than the wildtype.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from period analysis.

claim: AT1G51320 has a period 0.29 hr shorter than wildtype.
source: AT1G76920 and AT1G51320 both have shorter periods overall (0.76 and 0.29 hr shorter, respectively), while AT1G09650 has a subpopulation that is 0.61 hr shorter than the wildtype.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from period analysis.

claim: AT1G09650 has a subpopulation that is 0.61 hr shorter than the wildtype.
source: AT1G76920 and AT1G51320 both have shorter periods overall (0.76 and 0.29 hr shorter, respectively), while AT1G09650 has a subpopulation that is 0.61 hr shorter than the wildtype.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from subpopulation analysis.

claim: ACF3 has no known protein recognition domain.
source: No publications exist regarding the functions of ACF3, which also has no known protein recognition domain.
evidence: This is stated as background information.

claim: ACF3 contains a close homolog AT1G20803 with an E-value of 1.6 × 10−87.
source: ACF3 contains a close homolog (AT1G20803 – E-value of 1.6 × 10−87) which may be why it was not identified in previous forward genetic screens (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Expression of ACF3 is not controlled by the circadian clock or diurnal cycles.
source: Expression of ACF3 is not controlled by the circadian clock or diurnal cycles (Mockler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression data analysis with a citation.

claim: ACF4 contains a Kelch-repeat domain.
source: ACF4, which contains a Kelch-repeat domain, also has no described mutant phenotype, and is only described in an overview of the Kelch-repeat containing F-box proteins in Arabidopsis (Andrade et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a description of the protein domain in ACF4.

claim: ACF4 has no described mutant phenotype.
source: ACF4, which contains a Kelch-repeat domain, also has no described mutant phenotype, and is only described in an overview of the Kelch-repeat containing F-box proteins in Arabidopsis (Andrade et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as background information with a citation.

claim: The closest homolog to ACF4 is AT3G46050 with an E-value of 2.5 × 10−59.
source: The closest homolog to ACF4 (AT3G46050 – E-value of 2.5 × 10−59) has not been studied (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: ACF4 is not controlled by the circadian clock or light cycles.
source: As with ACF3, ACF4 is not controlled by the circadian clock or light cycles (Mockler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression data analysis with a citation.

claim: ACF5 has a predicted FBA3 domain.
source: Very little is known about ACF5 outside of its predicted FBA3 domain.
evidence: This is a description of the protein domain in ACF5.

claim: No expression data is available for ACF5.
source: No expression data, either diurnal or circadian regulation or tissue-specific, is available for ACF5 (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated based on database searches.

claim: ACF5 has some homology to AT1G47790 with an E-value of 1.2 × 10−102.
source: It has some homology to other genes (AT1G47790 – E-value of 1.2 × 10−102), which again indicates that it may have been missed in previous genetic screens due to redundancy.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Two U-box decoy populations had average period lengths longer than wild type.
source: We found that two populations of decoy plants had average period lengths longer than wild type, AT2G33340 (1.31 hr longer) and AT5G62560 (0.37 hr longer) (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 1.09 × 10−3) (Figure 8, marked with stars and pink gene names) making AT2G33340 the only U-box decoy with a major effect on the average period difference.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: AT2G33340 decoy population has a period 1.31 hr longer than wild type.
source: We found that two populations of decoy plants had average period lengths longer than wild type, AT2G33340 (1.31 hr longer) and AT5G62560 (0.37 hr longer) (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 1.09 × 10−3) (Figure 8, marked with stars and pink gene names) making AT2G33340 the only U-box decoy with a major effect on the average period difference.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from period analysis.

claim: AT5G62560 decoy population has a period 0.37 hr longer than wild type.
source: We found that two populations of decoy plants had average period lengths longer than wild type, AT2G33340 (1.31 hr longer) and AT5G62560 (0.37 hr longer) (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 1.09 × 10−3) (Figure 8, marked with stars and pink gene names) making AT2G33340 the only U-box decoy with a major effect on the average period difference.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from period analysis.

claim: AT2G33340 is the only U-box decoy with a major effect on the average period difference.
source: We found that two populations of decoy plants had average period lengths longer than wild type, AT2G33340 (1.31 hr longer) and AT5G62560 (0.37 hr longer) (Welch's t-test with a Bonferroni corrected α of 1.09 × 10−3) (Figure 8, marked with stars and pink gene names) making AT2G33340 the only U-box decoy with a major effect on the average period difference.
evidence: This is a result from period analysis.

claim: Three U-box decoy populations had subpopulations that were different from the parental control: AT3G49810, PUB48, and AT1G04510.
source: Three additional U-box decoy populations had subpopulations that were different from the parental control, AT3G49810, PUB48, and AT1G04510 (Figure 8, marked with daggers and blue gene names).
evidence: This is a result from subpopulation analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: AT3G49810 has one subpopulation which is 1.11 hr longer than the wildtype.
source: AT3G49810 has one subpopulation which is 1.11 hr longer than the wildtype (n = 7), while the other subpopulation is not significantly different (n = 32).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from subpopulation analysis.

claim: PUB48 has one subpopulation which is 2.20 hr longer than the wildtype.
source: Similarly, PUB48 has one subpopulation which is 2.20 hr longer than the wildtype (n = 4), and a second subpopulation which is not significantly different (n = 48).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from subpopulation analysis.

claim: AT1G04510 has one subpopulation that is 1.75 hr longer than wildtype.
source: AT1G04510 is different in that it has one subpopulation that we consider in the major effect category (1.75 hr longer, n = 15), and one that is short period (0.4 hr shorter, n = 14).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from subpopulation analysis.

claim: AT1G04510 has one subpopulation that is 0.4 hr shorter than wildtype.
source: AT1G04510 is different in that it has one subpopulation that we consider in the major effect category (1.75 hr longer, n = 15), and one that is short period (0.4 hr shorter, n = 14).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from subpopulation analysis.

claim: PUB30 (AT3G49810) contains two armadillo (ARM) repeats.
source: AT3G49810, also known as PUB30, contains two armadillo (ARM) repeats and has a potential homolog, PUB31 (AT5G65920; E-value of 1.2 × 10−171, Table 3).
evidence: This is a description of the protein domains in PUB30.

claim: PUB30 has a potential homolog PUB31 (AT5G65920) with an E-value of 1.2 × 10−171.
source: AT3G49810, also known as PUB30, contains two armadillo (ARM) repeats and has a potential homolog, PUB31 (AT5G65920; E-value of 1.2 × 10−171, Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: PUB30 expression is rhythmic under diurnal conditions and under one of the circadian conditions.
source: PUB30 expression is rhythmic under diurnal conditions and under one of the circadian conditions (Mockler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression data analysis with a citation.

claim: PUB30 is expressed globally.
source: Both tissue expression maps suggest that PUB30 is expressed globally (Klepikova et al., 2016; Winter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression atlas data with citations.

claim: PUB30 has a described function in inhibiting the salt stress response.
source: PUB30 has a described function in inhibiting the salt stress response (Hwang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: PUB48 (AT5G18340) contains two ARM repeats.
source: AT5G18340 is known as PUB48, and, like PUB30, contains two ARM repeats and has a partially redundant homolog, PUB46 (AT5G18320, E-value of 3.8 × 10−127, Table 3) (Adler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the protein domains in PUB48 with a citation.

claim: PUB48 has a partially redundant homolog PUB46 (AT5G18320) with an E-value of 3.8 × 10−127.
source: AT5G18340 is known as PUB48, and, like PUB30, contains two ARM repeats and has a partially redundant homolog, PUB46 (AT5G18320, E-value of 3.8 × 10−127, Table 3) (Adler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis shown in Table 3 with a citation.

claim: PUB48 expression is not rhythmic under diurnal cycles.
source: PUB48 expression is not rhythmic under diurnal cycles.
evidence: This is based on expression data analysis.

claim: PUB48 is rhythmic under circadian conditions in two out of three available experiments.
source: Interestingly, it is rhythmic under circadian conditions in two out of three available experiments, and has a similar phase in both (ZT14 and ZT17).
evidence: This is based on expression data analysis.

claim: PUB48 is expressed globally, although it exhibits some enrichment in floral buds and potentially senescent leaves.
source: Expression profiling suggests that PUB48 is expressed globally, although it exhibits some enrichment in floral buds and potentially senescent leaves (Klepikova et al., 2016; Winter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression atlas data with citations.

claim: PUB48 positively regulates the response to drought stress.
source: PUB48 is also involved in stress responses, as it has been shown to positively regulate the response to drought stress (Adler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: MAC3A (AT1G04510) and MAC3B (AT2G33340) both contain 7 WD repeats.
source: AT1G04510 and AT2G33340 are also known as MAC3A and MAC3B, respectively. MAC3A and MAC3B both contain 7 WD repeats, are 82% identical at the protein sequence level, and are known to act redundantly (Table 3) (Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the protein domains with a citation.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B are 82% identical at the protein sequence level.
source: AT1G04510 and AT2G33340 are also known as MAC3A and MAC3B, respectively. MAC3A and MAC3B both contain 7 WD repeats, are 82% identical at the protein sequence level, and are known to act redundantly (Table 3) (Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence analysis with a citation.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B are known to act redundantly.
source: AT1G04510 and AT2G33340 are also known as MAC3A and MAC3B, respectively. MAC3A and MAC3B both contain 7 WD repeats, are 82% identical at the protein sequence level, and are known to act redundantly (Table 3) (Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: MAC3A cycles under diurnal conditions.
source: While both cycle under one of the circadian conditions, only MAC3A cycles under diurnal conditions (Mockler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression data analysis with a citation.

claim: Both MAC3A and MAC3B are expressed globally.
source: Tissue-specific expression profiles are very similar for the two genes, as both are expressed globally (Klepikova et al., 2016; Winter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on expression atlas data with citations.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B are orthologous to the human and yeast Pre-mRNA Processing factor 19 (PRP19) proteins.
source: MAC3A and MAC3B are orthologous to the human and yeast Pre-mRNA Processing factor 19 (PRP19) proteins, the central components of the spliceosome activation machinery known as the Nineteen Complex (NTC) (Chanarat and Sträßer, 2013; Hogg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B were initially identified as regulators of plant immunity.
source: In plants, they were initially identified regulators of plant immunity, but further work confirmed their roles in the regulation of splicing and miRNA biogenesis (Jia et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B have roles in the regulation of splicing and miRNA biogenesis.
source: In plants, they were initially identified regulators of plant immunity, but further work confirmed their roles in the regulation of splicing and miRNA biogenesis (Jia et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Splicing is a critical regulatory step in plant clock function.
source: Accordingly, splicing is a critical regulatory step in plant clock function (Filichkin and Mockler, 2012; Park et al., 2012; Sanchez et al., 2010; Simpson et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mac3a and mac3b single mutants alone have little effect on the period, amplitude, or phase of the circadian clock.
source: The mac3a and mac3b single mutants alone have little effect on the period, amplitude, or phase of the circadian clock (Figure 10A–D) suggesting their functions may be redundant.
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 10A-D.

claim: The mac3a/mac3b double mutant has a significant phase delay.
source: Unlike the single mutants, the mac3a/mac3b double mutant has a significant phase delay (Figure 10E–F).
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 10E-F.

claim: The mac3a/mac3b double mutant has a phase delay of 3.95 hr for TOC1 expression.
source: The mac3a/mac3b double mutant has a phase delay of 3.95 hr for TOC1 expression and 5.90 hr for CCA1 expression (Figure 10G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FFT-NLLS analysis shown in Figure 10G.

claim: The mac3a/mac3b double mutant has a phase delay of 5.90 hr for CCA1 expression.
source: The mac3a/mac3b double mutant has a phase delay of 3.95 hr for TOC1 expression and 5.90 hr for CCA1 expression (Figure 10G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FFT-NLLS analysis shown in Figure 10G.

claim: The phase delay in CCA1 expression in the mac3a/mac3b double mutant is statistically significant.
source: While the phase delay in CCA1 expression is statistically significant, we do not reach statistical significance for the TOC1 phase delay.
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis.

claim: The TOC1 phase delay in the mac3a/mac3b double mutant does not reach statistical significance.
source: While the phase delay in CCA1 expression is statistically significant, we do not reach statistical significance for the TOC1 phase delay.
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis.

claim: A secondary peak appears in TOC1 expression in the mac3a/mac3b double mutant.
source: This is likely due to the appearance of a secondary peak in TOC1 expression in the mac3a/mac3b double mutant that makes phase calls difficult (Figure 10F).
evidence: This is an observation from the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B are the first U-box genes identified as regulators of the circadian clock in any system.
source: Together, this suggests that MAC3A and MAC3B are bona fide regulators of the circadian clock, and the first U-box genes, to our knowledge, identified as regulators of the circadian clock in any system.
evidence: This is stated as a key contribution of the work.

claim: The absence of a clock phenotype in the mac3a and mac3b single mutants demonstrates the genes are redundant.
source: Furthermore, the absence of a clock phenotype in the mac3a and mac3b single mutants demonstrates the genes are redundant, and highlights the strength of the decoy technique to overcome traditional genetic barriers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data.

claim: The mac3a/mac3b mutant exhibits global splicing defects and intron retention.
source: As the mac3a/mac3b mutant was recently shown to exhibit global splicing defects and intron retention, we hypothesized that these splicing defects may impact the circadian clock.
evidence: This is stated as background for the splicing experiments.

claim: SKIP, another component of the NTC, has a lengthened circadian period when mutated.
source: Like MAC3A and MAC3B, another component of the NTC, SNW/SKI-interacting protein (SKIP), has a lengthened circadian period when mutated, likely due in part to the dysregulation of PRR9 and PRR7 splicing (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant there is a decrease in the amplitude of the active PRR9 spliceoform PRR9a.
source: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant we observe a decrease in the amplitude of the active PRR9 spliceoform, termed PRR9a, as well a secondary inactive form, referred to as PRR9b (Figure 11A–B).
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 11A-B.

claim: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant there is a decrease in the amplitude of the inactive PRR9 spliceoform PRR9b.
source: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant we observe a decrease in the amplitude of the active PRR9 spliceoform, termed PRR9a, as well a secondary inactive form, referred to as PRR9b (Figure 11A–B).
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 11A-B.

claim: In the mac3a/mac3b mutant there is an increase in the average amplitude of the inactive spliceoform PRR9c, which retains an intron inappropriately.
source: This is accompanied by an increase in the average amplitude of the inactive spliceoform, PRR9c, which retains an intron inappropriately (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Accurate expression of genes involved in the circadian clock is essential to maintaining 24 hr periodicity.
source: Accurate expression of genes involved in the circadian clock is essential to maintaining 24 hr periodicity (Más et al., 2003; Rawat et al., 2011; Somers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Constitutive expression of full-length MAC3B causes period lengthening similar to mac3a/mac3b double mutant.
source: Interestingly, constitutive expression of the full-length MAC3B causes period lengthening similar to mac3a/mac3b double mutant (Figure 12).
evidence: This is a result from circadian period measurements shown in Figure 12.

claim: Maintaining proper expression of MAC3B is necessary for clock function.
source: This indicates that maintaining proper expression of MAC3B is necessary for clock function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overexpression data.

claim: F-box decoy proteins are able to interact with target proteins and regulatory partners and retain the ability to form biologically relevant complexes.
source: We have previously shown that F-box decoy proteins are able to interact with target proteins and regulatory partners and retain the ability to form biologically relevant complexes (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Five known components of the plant NTC were identified in the MAC3B IP-MS experiments in addition to the MAC3B bait peptides.
source: We compared this list to the previously identified components of the plant NTC, and identified five common components in addition to the MAC3B bait peptides, three of which (MAC3A, CELL DIVISION CYCLE 5 (CDC5), and MODIFIER OF SNC1,4 (MOS4)) were only found in the MAC3B IP-MS experiments and not in the controls (Table 4) (Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a result from IP-MS experiments shown in Table 4.

claim: MAC3A, CDC5, and MOS4 were only found in the MAC3B IP-MS experiments and not in the controls.
source: We compared this list to the previously identified components of the plant NTC, and identified five common components in addition to the MAC3B bait peptides, three of which (MAC3A, CELL DIVISION CYCLE 5 (CDC5), and MODIFIER OF SNC1,4 (MOS4)) were only found in the MAC3B IP-MS experiments and not in the controls (Table 4) (Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a result from IP-MS experiments shown in Table 4.

claim: The MAC3B decoy is capable of forming biologically relevant complexes in vivo.
source: This data suggests that the MAC3B decoy is capable of forming biologically relevant complexes in vivo and importantly supports the idea that the decoy strategy can be used for genetic and biochemical analyses of E3 ligase function in plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IP-MS data.

claim: MAC3A and MAC3B were observed interacting in the IP/MS data.
source: We observed MAC3A and MAC3B interacting in our IP/MS data and PRP19, the MAC3A and MAC3B orthologue from yeast and humans, is predicted to form a tetramer (Grillari et al., 2005; Ohi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a result from IP-MS experiments with citations.

claim: PRP19 is predicted to form a tetramer.
source: We observed MAC3A and MAC3B interacting in our IP/MS data and PRP19, the MAC3A and MAC3B orthologue from yeast and humans, is predicted to form a tetramer (Grillari et al., 2005; Ohi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Tetramer formation of PRP19 is predicted to be mediated by a conserved coiled coil.
source: Tetramer formation is predicted to be mediated by a conserved coiled coil that is present in MAC3A and MAC3B (Li et al., 2018), and was included in our MAC3A and MAC3B decoy constructs (Figure 12).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 12.

claim: The conserved coiled coil is present in MAC3A and MAC3B.
source: Tetramer formation is predicted to be mediated by a conserved coiled coil that is present in MAC3A and MAC3B (Li et al., 2018), and was included in our MAC3A and MAC3B decoy constructs (Figure 12).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Constitutive expression of the MAC3B WD domain causes two subpopulations of transgenic plants, one with lengthened period (25.5 hr) and one with shortened period (22.5 hr).
source: Constitutive expression of the MAC3B WD domain causes two subpopulations of transgenic plants, one with lengthened period (25.5 hr) and one with shortened period (22.5 hr) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is a result from circadian period measurements shown in Figure 12.

claim: The MAC3B WD phenotype more closely resembles the MAC3A decoy phenotype.
source: Interestingly, the MAC3B WD phenotype more closely resembles the MAC3A decoy phenotype, suggesting that MAC3A and MAC3B may have diverged slightly in their biochemical function or oligomerization capabilities.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing phenotypes.

claim: Oligomerization plays an important role in MAC3B function in the clock.
source: This was different than expressing the decoy or full-length MAC3B and indicates that oligomerization plays an important role in MAC3B function in the clock.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MAC3B WD data.
